metadata.title: ChatGPT: The brightest student in the class

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a small, purpose-built experimental design rather than an ILSA microdata sample with complex survey sampling. Students (n=30) and teachers (n=30) were recruited from five Spanish secondary-school centers and five Spanish regions, and texts were scored using a provided rubric (content and style). The manuscript does not report any use of sampling/survey weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis relies on descriptive and inferential tests (t-test/ANOVA) rather than PV-based achievement estimation. Therefore, no ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are applicable; results should be interpreted as experimental comparisons within this recruited sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not analyze PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes from PISA; instead, it compares teacher-assigned rubric scores for a ChatGPT-generated summary versus summaries written by recruited 15-year-old students. Because the dependent variables are rubric-based content/style scores from an experimental scoring task (not PV achievement scales), plausible values are not applicable. The paper also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusions beyond teacher consent rejection), so the missing-data strategy is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is constructed in four phases: (1) recruit 30 Spanish students aged 14–16 (16 females, 14 males) from five secondary-school centers; (2) use a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text (385 words) and have students write summaries capped at 125 words; (3) generate one ChatGPT summary using a prompt to act as a 15-year-old and keep the same 125-word limit, then camouflage this summary among the students’ summaries; (4) recruit 51 Spanish language teachers across five regions and exclude 21 teachers (5 for not providing informed consent and 16 to create a homogeneous teacher sample by sex/age/experience), leaving 30 teachers who scored all summaries using a rubric with two dimensions (content and style).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading comprehension text (summary task; 15-year-old students)
main_findings.target_variable: Summary evaluation (style score difference: ChatGPT vs students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: t-test/ANOVA results reported: style differences between ChatGPT and students all > 3 points; gender effect not significant (p > 0.05); teacher age effect significant (p < 0.05; older teachers show larger differences); experience effect not significant (p > 0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading comprehension text data embedded in a classroom summary task, the study leveraged teacher gender, teacher age, and teacher experience to evaluate the style-score difference between a ChatGPT-generated summary and real students’ summaries, finding that ChatGPT’s style scores exceeded students’ by more than 3 points on average. This indicates that, in pre-university writing tasks, generative AI can produce stylistically strong outputs that may be systematically over-rewarded unless assessment practices explicitly target authenticity and critical processing.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 Reading comprehension text (summary task; 15-year-old students)
main_findings.target_variable: Summary evaluation (content score difference: ChatGPT vs students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: t-test/ANOVA results reported: content differences between ChatGPT and students all > 2.5 points; gender effect significant (p < 0.05; larger differences for men); teacher age effect significant (p < 0.05; younger teachers show smaller differences); experience effect not significant (p > 0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 Reading comprehension text data embedded in a classroom summary task, the study leveraged teacher gender, teacher age, and teacher experience to evaluate the content-score difference between a ChatGPT-generated summary and real students’ summaries, finding that ChatGPT’s content scores exceeded students’ by more than 2.5 points on average. This indicates that content-focused rubric scoring may also be vulnerable to generative AI advantages, suggesting that policy and practice should incorporate methodological safeguards (e.g., process-based evidence, critical comparison requirements) rather than relying solely on final-text quality.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a PISA 2009 reading comprehension text as the source material for a classroom summary task with recruited Spanish 14–16-year-old students (n=30) and a camouflaged ChatGPT-generated summary. Thirty Spanish language teachers (after excluding 21 of 51 for consent and sample-homogenization reasons) scored all summaries using a rubric with two dimensions: content and style. The results show that ChatGPT’s summaries received higher teacher scores than the best real student summaries, with style differences exceeding 3 points and content differences exceeding 2.5 points. Teacher characteristics moderated these differences: gender and teacher age showed significant effects (p<0.05), while teacher experience did not (p>0.05). The analysis is based on t-tests/one-factor ANOVA rather than ML prediction, and the paper does not report any missing-data handling strategy or survey-weighting approach.
